title: Nostalgia and Tonic
gist: Nick Danforth uses gin branding (Gordon's, Bombay Sapphire, Beefeater, Fever-Tree) to illustrate Hobsbawm's 'invented traditions': imperial nostalgia sells even when the brand postdates the empire. He warns that nationalists and also liberal scholars distort the past through nostalgia.

insights.claim: Imperial nostalgia is a potent branding force even when the brand postdates the empire: Bombay Sapphire, launched in 1986, uses Bombay, Queen Victoria and a sapphire from British Ceylon to evoke the British Empire.
insights.speaker: Nick Danforth
insights.so_what: Heritage storytelling can support premium pricing (about $25 vs about $15 a bottle in the US) regardless of real provenance.
insights.quote: Imperial nostalgia is a potent branding force—even when the brand in question postdates the empire itself.
insights.locator: Imperial nostalgia is a potent branding force

insights.claim: Gordon's, founded in 1769 and tied to the Royal Navy, is genuinely historic, while Beefeater (1876), Old Raj (1972), Broker's (1998) and Bombay Sapphire (1986) layer faux or meta-historic nostalgia on top.
insights.speaker: Nick Danforth
insights.so_what: Brand age claims range from authentic to invented; authenticity does not map to price tier.

insights.claim: Hobsbawm's insight is that customs become 'tradition' only once circumstances change: wigs, royal carriages and the gin and tonic are enjoyed as tradition precisely when the original need (such as malaria risk) is gone.
insights.speaker: Nick Danforth
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for consumer-brand heritage: nostalgia monetizes the disappearance of the original function.
insights.quote: it is precisely when you no longer have to worry about dying of malaria that you can best enjoy a traditional gin and tonic
insights.locator: When discussing tradition, invented and otherwise

insights.claim: There is no evidence the gin and tonic was invented by British officers in India or that Churchill uttered the popular quote about it, which appears to have been invented online in the early 2010s.
insights.speaker: Nick Danforth
insights.so_what: Viral heritage claims should be checked before being used in marketing or analysis.

insights.claim: Historical myths matter most to right-wing nationalists, who imagine their countries as more ancient and virtuous than they were, and imperial nostalgia in Britain, France, Turkey, Russia and the US can feed racism and revanchism.
insights.speaker: Nick Danforth
insights.so_what: Nostalgic imperial narratives are a political driver to monitor in nationalist movements.

insights.claim: Debunking national food myths (pizza, tiramisu, carbonara) has caused more national soul-searching in Italy than critiques of the Magna Carta in Britain.
insights.speaker: Nick Danforth
insights.so_what: Cultural identity attached to everyday goods can be more emotionally charged than attachment to political symbols.

insights.claim: Liberal and progressive scholars also fall prey to ahistoric nostalgia, romanticizing the pre-Trump United States as more democratic and diverse than it was, or imagining pre-nationalist eras with open borders.
insights.speaker: Nick Danforth
insights.so_what: Both camps rely on idealized pasts, so political narratives on all sides should be discounted for nostalgia.
